cards.front: Describe the two stages of gene expression, in order.
cards.back: **Transcription** copies a gene into mRNA using one DNA strand as a template, in the nucleus of a eukaryotic cell. **Translation** then reads the mRNA at a ribosome to build a polypeptide.
cards.hint: Start with the molecule the cell makes first from the gene.

cards.front: How can a single base substitution have three different effects on a polypeptide?
cards.back: The new codon may code for the **same amino acid** (silent), a **different amino acid** (missense), or a **stop codon** (nonsense), which ends translation early and gives a shorter polypeptide.
cards.hint: Think about what the new codon codes for.

cards.front: Why does deleting one base usually have a much bigger effect than swapping one base?
cards.back: Codons are read in **triplets**, so deleting one base shifts the reading frame and every later codon changes. A substitution changes at most one codon.
cards.hint: Count how many codons each change alters.

cards.back: A **gene** is a sequence of DNA that influences a characteristic. Many genes code for a polypeptide.
A **codon** is a triplet of bases in mRNA that specifies one amino acid or a stop signal.
cards.hint: Think about how many bases are read at a time.

cards.front: What do tRNA molecules do during translation?
cards.back: tRNA carries an **amino acid** to the ribosome. Its anticodon is complementary to the mRNA codon, and peptide bonds then join the amino acids.
cards.hint: Think about how each amino acid is matched to the mRNA.

cards.front: A student says a mutation in any body cell will be passed on to the next generation. What is wrong?
cards.back: Only a mutation in a **gamete** may be inherited. A mutation in a body cell is not passed on to offspring.
cards.hint: Think about which cells form the next generation.

cards.front: In sickle cell disease, what does one base substitution change in the haemoglobin polypeptide?
cards.back: It changes **one amino acid**, which alters the properties of the haemoglobin molecule.

cards.front: What happens to the polypeptide if three bases are added or removed instead of one?
cards.back: The **reading frame** is kept, so only one amino acid is added or removed and the rest of the sequence stays the same.
cards.hint: Compare how many codons are affected with a frameshift.

cards.back: A **transcription factor** is a protein that binds to DNA near a gene and increases or decreases its transcription.

cards.front: How does lactose switch on the lac operon genes in bacteria?
cards.back: Lactose binds to the **repressor** and changes its shape. The repressor then releases the DNA, so the genes can be transcribed.
cards.hint: Think about what the repressor does when nothing else is bound to it.

cards.back: A **regulatory gene** with a homeobox sequence of about $180\,\text{bp}$. Its product binds DNA and switches on other genes that control development.
cards.hint: Compare it with the regulatory genes you have just met.

cards.front: How do different homeobox genes produce different structures along the head-to-tail axis?
cards.back: Each homeobox gene is **expressed in a particular part** of the embryo, so each part develops its own structures.
cards.hint: Think about where along the body each gene is switched on.

cards.back: **Apoptosis** is programmed cell death, in which a cell is dismantled in a controlled way. In a human embryo it separates the fingers and toes.
